newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt rounds up 34 suspected Moslem outlaws.
newsitem.headline: Egypt rounds up 34 suspected Moslem outlaws.

text.p: Authorities have arrested 34 people suspected of belonging to Egypt's most influential but outlawed fundamentalist group, the Moslem Brotherhood, a security source said on Sunday.

"The State Security Bureau of Investigation foiled a new plan by the outlawed Moslem Brotherhood group to prepare new student cadres...and penetrate universities to spread Brotherhood ideas," he told Reuters.
He said the 34 were arrested on Saturday at a flat in the Mediterranean city of Alexandria, which they were alleged to have used as a training camp.
The group's spokesman Mamoun Hudaibi denied the plans.
"How can 34 people train in a flat? It would be like a sardine tin," said Hudaibi. "It is clear that they were some poor students who went to Alexandria on a holiday."

The security source said the detained were from several provinces. "Large quantities of leaflets and organisational documents on movements and ways to recruit more elements...were seized in the flat," he said.
The prosecutor's office on Sunday was interrogating the detainees and by mid-day had ordered 13 held for 15 days, the security source said.
Hudaibi said the allegations were part of the Interior Ministry's campaign against the group, linking them to a recent attack on an opposition paper.

"We say clearly that the Interior Ministry condemned and exposed itself about two weeks ago...when it complained to the state prosecutor against the daily Al-Shaab for publishing corruption accusations against the interior minister.
"It said that the Moslem Brotherhood was behind Al-Shaab's campaign and that the paper was the Brotherhood mouthpiece," Hudaibi said.

The Moslem Brotherhood is the largest and most influential Islamic organisation in Egypt. It says it seeks to transform Egypt into a stricter Islamic state through democratic, peaceful means, including elections.
In this way it differs from the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), which has used violence in its bid for transformation.

More than 150 suspected militants, most of them accused of belonging to the Gama'a, are on trial in military and state security courts in what analysts see as the government's final blow in its fight against Moslem militant groups.

Another 35 suspected militants were referred on July 31 to state security court on charges of belonging to an outlawed group, the charge sheet received by Reuters on Sunday said. The date for the start of their trial has not yet been set.
Moslem militants have been fighting the government since 1992 to establish a strict Islamic state. More than 1,000 people have been killed.
